This can be used for takeoff or emer gency power and allows a motor with 
lower rated power than an equi valent gasoline engine. Elect ric motor s 
don't lose power with altitude (although fuel cells do). Ele ctric aircraft also 
have a fairly flat torq ue-v s-rpm curve which makes it easier to use them 
for flight control, compared to fuel-burning engines. 
Aircraft configuration flexibility is enhanced with the use of electric pro­
pulsion. The motors are small and can be placed far away from the powe r 
supply. It has been proposed to use electrical generators and motors to remo­
tely locate the fans of turbofan engines out to the wings or another location 
deemed beneficial. Some electric aircraft designs use multiple small motors 
on the wing and feed them varying amounts of power to attain yaw 
control. In fact, most quadcopters have no controls at all other than 
varying the power to their four motors. 
Elect ric motors themsel ves have always been lighter than internal 
combustion engines and are getting even better. Thanks to the increased 
interest and research in aircraft electric power plants, the weight per unit 
power of motor plus housing and inverter has been halved in the last decade. 
There can even be a weight savings for the propeller. For a piston engine, 
the propeller is used as a flywheel to help damp out the intermittent "bangs" 
of the cylinders. This might require additional mass in the propeller that is 
avoided with an electric motor. Also, if a propeller extension shaft is used 
with a piston engine, that shaft will be prone to torsional excitation and 
will have to be made stronger and heavier as a result. Not so with an electric 
motor. Furthermore, the electric motor is smaller and it might be po ssible to 
move the motor closer to the propeller, eliminating the need for a shaft in the 
first place. At the least, the smaller size of an electric motor should allow a 
more streamlined cow ling. 
There are, of course, disadvantages or we would have been using them for 
years . While the motors are lighter, the total weight including the power 
supply is almost cer tainly heavier than an equival ent power, equivalent 
run-time internal com bustion engine. 
It usually takes longer to "refuel" an electric airplane, that is, recharge the 
batteries. Progress is being made both in recharge time and in alternative 
concepts such as fuel cells that don't involve recharging, but it is still a lot 
quicker to refill gas tanks. 
Elect ric propulsion systems currently cost more, especially if an exotic 
power supply is used. The coun ter argument is that the "fuel" cost per 
flight hour is much cheaper than gasoline so in effect, you are "purch asing" 
your fuel in advance. 
The elect ric motors often need reduction drives due to their high rpm, 
which adds to the weight, cost, and comple xity. Gea red reduction drives 
can make quite a bit of noise. 
A subtle disadvantage is that, unlike fuel-based powerplants, there is no 
range benefit from the burn off of "fuel" during the mission. At the end of 
cruise, the gas-p owered aircraft is lighter and therefore has less drag. It is 

===== PDF PAGE 773 =====
CHAP TE R 20 Ele ctri c Ai rcr aft 74 1 
this effect that is integrated in the Breguet range equation, but it does not 
apply to electric propulsion. In stead, drag stays the same and the range is 
found sim ply as speed times the power supply's calculated duration. For a 
long-range aircraft this may be equival ent to a 10- 20% reduction in range. 
For battery power systems there are additional problems. There are temp­
erature effects on the batteries, with loss of power if too hot or too cold. 
Attem pting to use the power at too high of a rate causes resistance losses, 
which reduces the total energy avail able. There is some risk of explosion 
and fire for certain battery types. Imagine all of the energy stored in a big 
battery being released all at once! And as every child with a flashlight has 
learned, batteries tend to lose power as they reach the end of their 
charge-j ust when we may need maximum power for a landing go-a round. 
Batteries don't last forever. They are limited both in calendar age and in 
total number of charge-discharge cycles. Complete battery replacement 
might be required every 5-8 years, or sooner if the plane is flown a lot. 
Most of us have experienced a perfectly good cellphone or laptop comp uter 
needing a battery replacement, and finding that the replacement cost is so 
high that a new unit is purchased instead. 
Hop efully this won't apply to electric airplanes. Toyota claims that not a 
single Prius automobile has required battery replacement due to failure to 
hold a charge. Toyota gets maximum life by ensuring that the batteries are 
never fully charged, nor fully discharged. This is probably not an option 
for airplanes, where weight is so impor tant that we cannot afford to oversize 
the battery pack as required by this strategy. 
Electric motors also put out a lot of stray electroma gnetic energy which 
can cause problems with other electronic componen ts. This author wit nessed 
the tragic demise of a 32-foo t-span unmanned research airplane const ructed 
as a senior design project. [2] This crashed because the electric motor 
interfered with the radio �ignals, including the signal to turn off the motor! 
Ele ctric power might not even be as "green" as imagined, when all things 
are considered. Any electrical power source other than solar cells will need to 
be charged or replenished. This means that there will be a ground facility 
some where creating that energy, probably from burning hydro carbon coal, 
oil, or natural gas. This off-vehicle pollution must be included in an honest 
system-level study of just how green an electric-powered airplane might 
be. Some skeptics prefer to call them "remote emissi on" rather than "zero 
emission" vehicle s. 
Also, certain materials used to make current batteries and solar cells are 
unfriendly to the environment, and their production and eventual disposal 
are of concern. Lithium is most ly extracted from salt lakebeds with huge, 
ugly processing plants using toxic solvents. Cobalt, used in the energy- dense 
NMC batteries, is both poisonous and carcinogenic causing pulmon ary, 
neurological, and respiratory problems. 
With all things consi dered, today's electric power cannot compete with 
gasoline engines for a "normal" aircraft doing "norma l" missions, in terms 

===== PDF PAGE 774 =====
742 Air craf t Design : A Concep tual Appro ach 
of attaining a certain spee d, range, and payload for a given weight or cost 
airplane. At least for now, electric power remains the province of small 
UA Vs, special-purpose airplanes, nontraditional missions, and fun alterna­
tives to the conventional approach. The technolog y is getting better, 
though, and the day may soon come when electric airplanes are com m on. 
Ele ctric Motor Basic s 
There are many options for aircraft electric propulsion. Elect ricity can be 
used to power a propeller, or a ducted fan, or even the compressor and/ or fan 
of a fuel-based turbine engine. The wild est conce pt, studied during the 19 60s, 
uses electro hydrodynamic forces (ionic discharge) to accelerate air through a 
mesh, creating noiseless thrust from a device with no mov ing parts. Unfortu­
nately, the electrical power required to create this thrust is 10-2 0 tim es 
higher than for a large- diameter propeller. f56l 
In most applications the power used for flight comes from an electric 
motor. These are quiet, smoot h, and highly reliabl e. They usually weigh 
less than eq uivalent power gas mot ors, even including the motor controller 
normally required. 
The first working direct current (DC) electric motor goes back to 18 2 7, 
and motors were in com mercial production a mere decade later. By 18 88, 
electric motors were a proven technolog y, and the first electric trolleys 
were entering service. That same year eccentric genius Nikola Tesla devel­
oped a practical alternating current (AC) motor. 
The basic idea of an electric motor consists of a nonmoving magnet ic 
object (" stator"), rigged to pull a rotating magnetic object ("rotor") in a circu­
lar path (Fig. 20. 1). Magnets have north and south poles just like the Earth, 
which actually is a magnet. Oppo site poles attract, whereas similar poles 
repel. The rotor and stator have north and south poles on opposi te sides of 
+ -
r-1� 
Fig. 20. 1 Electric motor schematic. 

===== PDF PAGE 775 =====
CHAPTER 20 Ele ctri c Aircraf t 743 
the rotation shaft, so that the rotor is being pulled in the proper direction 
from both sides. 
After the rotor has been pulled through a path of 180 deg, it would lock to 
the position closest to the pulling magnet so that the polarity of the pull is 
quickly reversed. The rotor then goes around another 180 deg, and the 
process continues. 
Either the rotor or the stator can be permanent magnets (lodestone or 
magnetized meta l), or either one can be electromagn ets, which are windings 
of wire through which a current is passed. At least one of them must be an 
electrom agnet so that its polar ity can be reversed. 
While electric motors are classed as DC or AC by the type of electrical 
current they can accept; inside they are all "alternating curren t." The 
current flow must alternate to reverse magnetic polarity to keep the rotor 
spinning around. In a DC motor, the "comm utator" swi tches the polarity 
of the current flow to the rotor windings depending on the rotor angle. 
Originally this switching was done by mechanical "brushes," which can 
literally resemble paint brushes made of wire resting against a rotating elec­
trical contact attached to the rotor. Brushes can also be metallic or graphite 
pads that are pressed against the contacts on the rotor. The current flow 
direction depends upon whi ch con tacts on the rotor are touching the 
brushes as it rotates around. 
In modern "brushless" motors, electronic circuits sense the rotor posi­
tion and switch the current flow. This impro ves efficiency and eliminates 
the brushes' high potential for sparking-a very bad thing espec ially in an 
airplane. 
The toy electric motors that we took apart as children are mostly DC, 
with permanent magnet stators outside and brushes supplying current to 
vary the polarity of the rotating electromagnets inside. This author had 
more success taking the111 apart than putting them back together. 
Electric motors for high-power applications more common ly have the 
current variation applied to electroma gnet stators, with the rotor being 
either permanent magnets or electro magnets whose polarity doesn't change. 
Also, practical motors often have the stators inside, with permanent 
magnets mounted to a "sq uirrel cage" rotor in a ring around the fixed 
stators. If you take apart that com puter in front of you, you'll probably find 
this "outrunner" arrangement in its cooling fan. 
Alternating current is just what it sounds like: the current flow const antly 
alternates from positive to negative, like household current which alternates 
at 50-60 cycles per second (crea ting the familiar hum when stray current 
vibrates hardware or enters sound circuit s). AC current doesn't have to be 
phase switched to power an electric motor; it already is. Because the switching 
is done by the current itself, the AC motor can norma lly run only at an rpm 
equal to that cycle rate or a submu ltiple of it. If the rotor is made of electromag­
nets, the current can be passed to it through brushes press ing on co ncentric 
rings. If the rotor uses permanent magnets, brushes are not required. 

===== PDF PAGE 776 =====
744 Ai rcraf t Desig n: A Conc eptu al Appr oach 
There is a problem with the "two -phase" motor described above, where 
the rotor gets pulled through a path of 18 0 deg and then the polarity is 
revers ed. If the rotor is lined up so that the rotor magnet poles are closest 
to the stator magnet poles, the magnetic pull is lined up with the axis of 
rotation so that there is no moment arm, thus no mo ment, thus no rotation. 
The rotor is stuck. Also, the moment arm approaches zero when the rotor 
poles approach the stator poles, so the torque drops towards zero twice in 
each revolution. 
To avoid these problems, the "thre e-phase" motor was invented (1 890 ) in 
wh ich additional electromagnets are located around the circumf erence, 
rigged to switch on and off approp riately to pull only when the geom etry 
gives a good moment arm. To make this happen, the alternating current 
itself has three oscillating sinuso idal waves, superimposed and transmi tted 
on the same wi res. 
Some electric motors have even more phases, giving better geomet ry and 
smo other oper ation at the exp ense of additiona l comp lexity. These can have 
so many different electromagnet locations that the rotor is pulled in its cir­
cular path by a magnetic attraction circling around like the fake rabbit that 
dashes around a dog race track, keeping just ahead of the dogs. 
A few points relevant to aircraft design: permanent magnet mot ors are 
more ef ficient than coil (elect romagnet) motors. Alternating current 
motors require AC power wh ereas batteries and solar cells are direct 
current, so a converter of some sort is required (us ually as a part of a 
motor controller). Motors using brushes are typically less efficient, and the 
likely sparking of brushes is a concern espec ially with hydrogen fuel cells. 
Brushless motors are usua lly more efficient and reliable, but need sophisti­
cated controllers to electro nically switch the current at the appropriate 
time so they cost a bit more. 
Brushless DC permanent magnet motors (BLDC-P M) are probably the 
best choice for aircraft applications given their better efficiency and weight, 
lack of sparking, and good torque characteristi cs. Their reliabil ity and 
safety are likely to be better because the rotating part does not have delicate 
wi res. They are used on the Pipistrel Taurus G4, winner of the NASA Green 
Flight Challenge, on the manned electric helicopter, and even on the 
self-balancing Segway Scoot er. 
Electric motors always need a "con troller" of some sort. This can range 
from an on-off switch to a sophisticated-and expen sive -piece of com puter­
driven high-power circuitry. Even an on-off sw itch will probably need 
overload protection and some scheme for starting the motor at a reduced 
voltage. Over-temperature sensing and shutoff is always a good idea. 
If the power supply is DC as for batteries, the controller will include a 
DC- AC inverter to produce the final current sent to the motor's electroma g­
nets. For this reason, controllers are some times ref erred to as "inverters. " By 
adjusting the length of time that current is provided during each rotation, the 
speed and power of the motor is controlled. 

===== PDF PAGE 777 =====
CH AP TER 20 El ectri c Air c raft 745 
A more-s ophisticated motor controller allows motor rotation to be 
reversed, or the motor can be convinced to work as a generator when 
slowing down or descending. This is equival ent to putting gasoline back 
into the tank when going downhi ll-a nice trick! 
Such moto r controllers are not cheap. They add 15 -35% to the motor's 
weight, and typically lose about 2% of the electrical energy as waste heat. 
These numbers are improving rapidly. An ongoing NASA research project 
has inverter/ controller goals of 12 kW /kg with 99% efficiency. 
� Power Suppl y: Batte rie s 
Electric motors are reliable and lightweight. The only problem is that they 
need electrical power, and all of the options weigh a lot more than a tank of 
gasoline. For the ion discharge test vehicle described above, the power supply 
was a long extension cord. More practical power supplies include batteries, 
fuel cells, solar cells, beamed energy, flywheels, or even a conventional 
engine coupled to an electrical generator, much like a diesel-ele ctric train. 
All have problems, and all suffer from relatively poor energy density. In 
other words, they weigh a lot for the power they can supply over a given 
amount of time. Hope for a fivefold breakthrough in stored energy 
density-it would change the world. 
Most electric airplanes fly using batteries. The word "battery" actually 
comes from none other than Ben Franklin, who was internation ally famous 
as a leading electrical experimenter long before his involvement in the Amer­
ican Revoluti on. Around 17 50, he was experimenting with Leyden jars, a 
recently invented way to store static electricity and a forerunner of today's 
capacitors and batteries. To increase total charge-holding ability, he con­
nected a number of them together. When discharged by completing the 
circuit (often through al! unsuspect ing turkey [57l), the Leyden jars would 
make a loud explosive noise, almost but not quite simultaneou sly, which 
Franklin compa red to the sound of an artillery battery of cannons. It was 
also Franklin who identified and named the positive and negative charges. l58l 
"Cell" is the proper terminolog y for a single unit that creates electricity 
from a chemical reaction. It has three parts: two electrodes, positive and 
negative and usually made of dissimilar metals, and the "ele ctroly te" which 
is a chemical surrounding and separating them. The electrol yte can be 
liquid or "dry" (act ually a paste). Strictly speaking, a "battery" is composed 
of one or more such "cells," but we common ly use the terms interchangeabl y. 
When the circuit is com pleted, ions (pos itively charged atoms) flow through 
the electrolyte one way, while electrons (negatively charged) flow out of the 
battery the other way, through the external circuit, and back to the other side 
of the battery. 
Franklin's experiments, like all others at that time, were done with static 
electricity produced by rubbing things together such as glass rubbed with 
one's own hands, or wool rubbed on am ber. In 18 00, Aless andro Volta 

===== PDF PAGE 778 =====
746 Aircr af t Desi gn: A Conceptual Approach 
invented the "artificial electric organ," a stack of alternating silver and zinc 
disks with saltwater-soaked cloth between them. Each pair of disks, separated 
by this simple electrolyte, made a cell, and the stack of them made a battery. 
The taller the stack, the more powerful the battery (more "volts," we now say). 
And unlike the Leyden jars that discharged instanta neousl y, these batteries 
could produce a steady current flow. 
Soon renamed the "Voltaic Pile, " it became the favorite tool of electrical 
experimenters who disco vered they could use it to amuse audiences, kill 
animals, explode gunpow der, and even separate water into oxygen and 
hydrogen. It was the popu lar fascination with applying electricity to recently 
dead animals that lead Mary Shelley to write her reanimation classic 
Frankenstein. 
To day's batteries are vastly impro ved over Volta 's. For one thing, Volta's 
batteries consumed their electrodes in the chemical reaction so that they 
were not rechargea ble. Other than the AA-p owered Oxyride described 
above, the batteries used today for aircraft are rechargeable (also called "sec­
ondary" batteries). Modern batteries have a vastly imp roved energy density, 
and their power stays relatively const ant as the cells are discharged. 
Yet still, we need significant improvement before battery- electric air­
planes can become truly comp etitive with fuel-based airplanes. Even after 
the superior efficiency of electric motors is included, gasoline has 20 times 
better effective energy density than the best batteries. f 59] 
The classic nickel- cadmium (NiCd, or "NiCad") rechargeable battery, 
invented in Sweden in 18 99, is now consi dered undes irable because the 
cadmium is toxic. They've been superseded by nickel- metal hydride 
(NiMH) batteries, wh ich have slightly better energy density. 
"Li-ion" is a catch- all phrase for a number of different lithium-based 
batteries, each using lithium plus other materials such as cobalt, manganese, 
or nickel. Lithium-ion batteries are common in consumer electronics and are 
currently the only batteries that are really practical for aircraft, automobiles, 
and other vehi cle applicat ions. They have better energy density than nickel­
based batteries and hold their charge for a long time, but present a fire hazard 
espe cially if they are shorted or charged too rapidly. 
Lithium polymer (LiPO) batteries are simply Li-ion batteries where the 
electrolyte is contained in a solid polymer compo site. This makes them 
lighter, and they can be formed into odd sha pes. They have the best energy 
dens ity of the readily available batteries for aircraft applications, weighing 
about 11 lb {5 kg} per kilow att-hour produced. They are also more rugged 
and reliable and can discharge at a high power level. Widely used in cell 
phones and model cars, planes, and helicopters, they are prone to explosion 
if short- circuited and to fire if punctured. 
NMC batteries, a type of Li-ion battery using lithium plus nickel, manga­
nese, and cobalt (oxide) are widely used for automobiles, electric ground 
vehicles, and high-end power tools. These have pretty good specific energy 
and overall performance for an "off the shelf' power supply. They we re

CHAP TER 20 El ectri c Ai rcraf t 747 
used by Solar Impulse 2 for its round-t he-w orld flight, to store the day's solar 
energy to allow flight throughout the night. Unfortunately, they overheated 
during the record-s etting Japan to Hawaii leg, grounding the airplane until 
new ones could be installed. 
Lithium-su lfur (Li-S) batteries show promise for the future. These are 
relatively lightweight and have higher energy dens ity than typical Li-ion 
batteries. Li-S batteries were used on the Boeing "S olar Eagle,'' a 400-ft 
{12 2 -m} span UA V designed to fly at high altitudes for a period of five years. 
Silver-zinc batteries have high energy density and are used in torpedoes 
and launch vehicl es. Silver-zinc batteries are exp ensive-check the ingredi­
ents list! Also, current versions don't survive many recharging cycles, but 
they have potential for the future. 
Zinc -air batteries are actually not rechargeable, but they are of great 
interest because they are fairly inexp ensive and have high energy dens ity 
both by weight and by volume. They work by reacting zinc with atmosp heric 
oxygen, essentially "breathing" to make electricity rather than using only 
chemicals contained within thems elves. This makes them relatively denser 
in energy terms. While they cannot be recharged by the simple application 
of current, they can be quickly refurbished by physically remo ving the 
spent zinc oxide and replacing it with fresh zinc. In some concepts this is 
done continuously, making them similar to fuel cells. 
Similarly, aluminum-air batteries offer great promise despite being 
"primary" batteries, i.e. non- rechargea ble. After each use they have to be 
refurbished by replacing the corroded aluminum cathode and rem oving 
the hydrated alumina residue. Clever design could make this a simple flight­
line operation, not much wo rse than topping off the oil of a piston engine. 
Aluminum-air batteries offer incredible specific energy, up to 8,0 00 Wh/ 
kg theoretically and as much as 1,3 00 Wh /kg in a "practical" application. 
Whether this includes th_e full weight of casing and required suppor t equip­
ment is unclear at this time. 
Startup comp any Ev iation is developing a more- attainable 400 Wh/kg 
proprietary system combin ing lithium-ion for high power operations and 
an aluminu m- air system for cruise and endurance. Their "Alice" design 
concept is a 9-passen ger commuter aircraft rese mbling the old Learfan, 
with V-tails, a pusher-prop at the back of the fuselage, and pusher electric 
motors at the wingt ips. All three motors are the 260 kW Siemens unit 
mentioned above. For the initial production version, conventional 
lithium-ion batteries of 220 Wh/kg are exp ected to provide a range of 
540 nm with reserves.

These approximate table values should not be exclusi vely relied upon 
for selection of battery type. You must also consider how many recharge 
cycles the battery can endure, the recharge rate (often 2-3 times slower 
than the discharge rate), temperature sens itivity, insulation and cooling 
requirements, fire hazard, system cost, handling issues, and the total 
system environm ental issues from mining the exotic metals to production 
to eventual disposal. 
The safety issues with batteries are always of concern. The more energy 
we can pack into a battery of a certain weight and volume, the more it 
resembles a bomb should all that energy be released at once! 
We know how to prevent that from happening. Like all parts put into an 
aircraft, the batteries must be properly constructed including excellent 
quality control and testing. Only credible and competent vendors should 
be used, and cheap "pirate" parts shouJd be ruthlessly avoided. A sophisti­
cated battery management system (BMS) must be used which monitors the 
batteries as to temperature during flight and during charging. Batteries 
should be charged at about 5-35 degC. Of course, the system design and 
physical installation must prevent shorting across the terminals during 
flight or ground handling. Remember the Apollo fire! 
r:J Power Suppl y: Fuel Cells 
Fuel cells are an attractive alternative to batteries for electric aircraft. 
They have high energy dens ity and are a well -proven technolog y. Even 
more impor tant, they can be quickly "recharged" by replacing the fuel as 
compared to a battery in which one hour of flight time may require three 
hours of recharging before the next flight. 
Fuel cells work by taking in a slow steady flow of a chemical and reacting 
it with an oxidizer, producing electricity as a byproduct. While natural gas 
and alcohols can be used, the normal fuel chemical is hydrogen, and the 
usual oxidizer is, in fact, atmospheric oxygen. The "exhaust" is then wate r. 
Hydrogen fuel cells have higher energy dens ity than the best batteries and 
are roughly twice as efficient as an internal combustion engine. They are 
commo nly used for spacecraft such as the Space Shuttle and have been 
flown in a number of manned and unmanned aircraft. Automobile compa­
nies are investing literally billions of dollars in fuel-cell car developme nt 
and expect to enter production in the next decade. 
Hydrogen is bulky unless stored under extreme pressure, making for 
heavy tanks. Unlike rechargeable batteries, you must purchase and pump 
the hydrogen. This is not currently available at most airports. Also, there is 
a lot of waste heat resulting in cooling air intakes about as large as for an 
equivalent piston engine airplane. Hy drogen is explosive and flammable, so 

===== PDF PAGE 782 =====
750 Ai rcraft Desig n: A Con cept ual Approach 
Fig. 20.2 Fuel-cell electric airplane powerplant. 
there is some extra risk from leaks and during crashes. Luckily, when freed it 
rises straight up rather than forming a flaming pool like petroleum fuels. 
There are several types of fuel cells including hydrogen proton exchange 
membrane (PEM), solid- oxide (SOFC), and the older alkaline fuel cell. Details 
are beyond the scope of this book, and the technolog y is rapidly improvin g. 
Figure 20.2 shows the powerplant of a fuel cell-electric airplane seen at 
the EAA AirVenture airshow and fly-in. The fuel cells are tucked underneath, 
to the right. The hydrogen tank is loca ted behind the cabin, and surge battery 
banks are in the wing leading edge. Note that the motor controller is big­
about the size of the actual motor (on the left, attached to the propeller). 
Powe r Suppl y: Hybr id-Electric 
Hy brid- electric power goes back to the 19 30's when trains and submar­
ines began using electric motors powered by diesel engines driving electrical 
generators. In some cases, the diesel engine could also directly drive the 
vehicle to avoid the conversion inefficiencies, but for simplic ity sake most 
of these vehicles used only the electric motors for the final drivetrain. 
For diesel- electric trains, still ubiquitous today, this hybrid power plant 
avoids the need for clutches and gearing, and provides smoot h torque in 
all conditions. When submerged, hybrid power allows submarines to be 
powered by batteries which are charged by the diesel engine while cruising 
on the surface. 
The hybrid-elec tric concept has a special benefit when applied to auto­
mobiles. Cars must accel erate quickly and occasio nally climb steep hills, 

===== PDF PAGE 783 =====
CHAPTER 20 Ele ctri c Air c raft 75 1 
but m ost of the time they need far less power. The fueled (gasoline) engine 
can be made smaller, being sized only for continuous cruising power 
needs. Battery power is used for surge needs. Better yet, the fueled engine 
can be shut off when the battery has enough charge to meet the current 
power needs, or when the car is stopped in traffic. This greatly increases 
overall fuel efficiency. Some hybrid cars even allow charging overnight 
through the ground power grid. If you don't travel long distances, you 
might go six mo nths without refilling the gas tank. 
Hybrid power might be the perfect power supply for electric airplanes, 
blending the smo othness and reliabil ity of an electric motor with the high 
energy content of a tank of gasoline. There are many options. The fueled 
engine can be piston or turbine, and the fuel can be gasoline, diesel, kerosene, 
methane, hydrogen, or others. Most hybrid concepts use batteries for energy 
storage and management, but they aren't required. 
There are several options for the drive train. A propeller or ducted fan can 
be driven solely by the electric motor, as in the subma rines, trains, and auto­
mobiles descr ibed above. This is called . "se ries hybrid" or in the automo tive 
world, "extended- range electric vehicles (E REV) ." In effect, the generator 
and electric motor replace the transmission of a conventionally- fueled 
engine, then batteries are added for additional capabilit ies. 
This approach takes advantage of the smoothness of an electric motor 
and allows the propeller or fan to be located away from the fueled engine. 
If the batteries are big enough, the aircraft can take off on battery power 
alone with benefits to noise and loca l pollution, or even fly for shorter mis­
sions without ever starting the fueled engine . 
Unfortunately, there is an efficiency loss of 10- 15% when the shaft power 
of the fueled engine is converted to elect ricity via a generator, and then back 
into shaft power by an electric motor. All this equipment weighs a lot more 
than the handful of bolts used to directly attach a propeller to a conventional 
engine. It adds to the volume inside the aircraft as well, leading to increased 
wetted area and airframe structural weight. 
On the other hand, perhaps the heavy flywheel built into a piston engine 
can be eliminated if the attached generator can serve the same damping func­
tion. Perhaps the generator can "work backward s" and serve as the starter 
motor. The propeller itself may be lighter if it doesn't have to be attached 
to a jerky internal combustion engine. With these savings and the inherently 
smaller fueled engine, there may be no net penalty or even a weight savings. 
Another drive train option is to use the electric motor as a "bo oster" for 
the fueled engine. The propeller is directly attached to the fueled engine as for 
a normal aircraft, with an electric motor either geared in (with clutch) or lit­
erally wr apped around the output shaft. The electric motor is also a genera­
tor, so it can be used to store energy in batteries when power demands are 
low, and can be used to add horsepo wer during takeoff and initial climb. 
Perhaps the batteries can be ground- charged before takeoff for an additional 
boost. 

===== PDF PAGE 784 =====
752 Aircr aft Des ign: A Concep tual Approach 
The main benefit of this "bo oster" approach is that it allows a sm aller 
fueled engine (and thus, lighter and cheaper). That smaller engine can be 
better matched to the lower power demands during cruise. The electric 
motor is also smaller than for the other hybrid concept since it doesn't 
have to power the aircraft all by itself. Note that this hybrid approach 
doesn't allow takeoff or flight on electric power alone. 
This "bo oster" approach is actually a variant of the "parallel hybrid" 
arrangement, in which the fueled or the electric motor can each drive the 
vehicle separately, or they can work together. This is used for several 
hybrid automobi les. For an aircraft this would require additional clutching, 
to disconnect the propeller from the fueled engine during electric -only flight. 
Yet another option, similar to the automoti ve "through-the-r oad 
(T TR)" hybrid, would have a conventional fueled engine with a dedicated 
propeller, and a compl etely separate electric motor with its own propeller. 
The aircraft could be flown on either propulsion system alone, or using 
both wh en maximum thrust is required. Prob ably the fueled engine 
would be attached to a generator to charge up the batteries for the electric 
motor. Clever design would be required to avoid large stopped- prop drag 
penalties. 
Some have proposed such a "through -the- air" hybrid arrangement using 
small electric motors on the wingtips in a pusher configuration. These would 
get extra thrust by "un wr apping" the rotation of the wingtip vortex. Unfortu­
nately, the prop blades wo uld cut through the wing wake causing vibration, 
noise, and loss of efficiency. Still, it may be a useful approach both for hybrid 
designs and for all-electric aircraft. 
There are several significant projects in work to develop hybrid-elec tric 
com mercial airliners. The regional aircraft market makes a logical application 
for hybrid- electric power. Although a ducted fan might look like a jet engine, 
it's really a propeller with a ring around it. These are more efficient at lower 
speeds and for shorter distances, but not for long range flight at near­
transonic speeds. 
With backing from Boeing, startup firm Zunum Aero is developing a 
12-s eat commercial hybrid- electric aircraft and has plans for designs of up 
to 50 seats. The Zuma concept is esse ntially a battery- powered electric 
fan aircraft much like hobby model airplanes, but with a 670 hp {500 kw} 
turboshaft engine buried in the fuselage for range extension. For takeoff 
and shorter missions the wi ng-mounted batteries, charged on the ground 
and quickly replaceable, are sufficient. 
The 12- seat Zunum design will weigh about 12, 500 lbs {5670 kg} and 
have a range of over 600 nmi {1,12 6 km} with a cruise speed of 300 kts 
{550 kph}. Cost is proj ected to be 8 cents per seat mile, versus around 25 
for current commuter aircraft. 
Airbus, in asso ciation with Rolls- Royce and Siemens, will flight-test a 
modified BAe 14 6 commuter aircraft with one of its four turbofans replaced 
with a 2700 hp {2,000 kw} electric motor driving a ducted fan. They plan to 

===== PDF PAGE 785 =====
CHA PTE R 20 Ele ctric Ai rcraf t 753 
apply hybrid-el ectric propulsion to future regional airliners of up to 100 
passengers. 
The recent EU HY PST AIR project has demonst rated an advanced 
hybrid-electric power system suitable for high-performance GA aircraft. 
The Siemens- developed 270 hp {200 kw} hybrid propulsion sys tem, based 
on a Rota x 91 4, was installed and ground-tested in a modified Pipistrel 
Panthera airframe. The generator exceeds 95% efficiency and only weighs 
about 7 kW /kg. The electric motor was attached to an efficient five-bladed, 
low-rpm propeller. Production of this exact design is not expected, but 
similar projects are in work. 
Power Supp ly: Solar Ce lls 
Another type of electrical power supply increasingly used for aircraft 
applications is the solar cell. These are panels that convert sunlight to elec­
tricity by the photovoltaic effect, first discovered in 18 39 and resulting in a 
working solar cell by 1883. Modern solar cells were introduced in 19 54 
and are related to transistors, being solid-st ate semicon ductor devices and 
usually made of crystalline silicon. While solar cells were hideou sly ex pensive 
just a few years ago, today they cost as little as a dollar per watt of solar-ce ll 
capability. The integration and control sy stem costs add a similar amount. 
Solar cells are well -proven for flight applications. They're just expensive 
and heavy. The first flight by solar cell alone was a large model airplane in 
19 74 called "S unrise I." Funded by DARPA, it flew for about 20 miles. 
The manned Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar cells. It used 
solar cells by day and lithium polymer batteries by night, with sufficient 
excess power to charge the batteries while flying during the day. The airplane 
is huge, with a wingspan of236 ft {7 1. 9 m}. The round-t he-world trip took 23 
days and nights of flight ttme, spread out over many mon ths due to technical 
and weather issues. (The similar Solar Impulse 1 is shown in Fig. 20.3.)

===== PDF PAGE 786 =====

Idea lly, solar cells should attain about 0. 1 kW of power per squa re fo ot 
{1.1 kW /m2 }, but we are far from that. Current efficiencies give abo ut 
0.02 kW /ft2 {0.2 1 kW /m2 }, so it takes almost 40 ft2 to obtain 1 hp in equiv­
alent elec tricity {"-'5 m 2 to give 1 kW} . They typically weigh about 0. 06 psf 
{0.3 kg/m2 }. Efficiencies are impro ving rapidly, so don't use these values 
for your design. Note that solar cells don't age well, losing over 1 % efficiency 
per year when in service. 
There is a subst antial installation weight for solar cells, almost doubling 
the cell weight. Also, they are not formed to the desired airfoil contour, so 
they can affect the airflow and make it difficult to maintain lamin ar flow. 
Solar cells printed on flexible plastic sheet are in development and offer 
both reduced weight and smoot her airfoil contours. 
When calcula ting the power obtained from solar cells, don't forget the 
time of day! Maximum power is obtained only at "high noon." There is a sinu­
soidal drop-off during the other daylight hours, and, of course, no power at 
night. The climate and latitude of flight also matter, along with the obvious 
time of year. Atmospheric vapor affects the amount of power obtained. 
Flight in northern Sweden in late De cember won't be as easy as flight over 
southern Somalia. 
Pointing must be considered. The solar power depends upon the 
projected area of the cells, measured in the direction of the sun (sine func­
tion). For that flight in northern Sweden, or for flight just after dawn or 
just before dusk, the top of the wings is a bad loca tion for the solar cells. 
Some solar-p owered airplanes have added non- lifting solar cell panels that 
can be aimed at the sun, or even wings that buckle into a saw tooth shape 
when seen from the front. 
There is an altitude effect as well, with high altitudes generally being 
favorable. There is less air to filter out the sunlight, less moist ure in the 
air, and less conc ern about clouds. There is no concern if you are high 
enough! This amounts to roughly 30% more available solar power outside 
the atmo sphere vs at sea level. 
Lecture notes [60] by Noth, Siegwart, and Engel detail the design of solar­
powered aircraft including solar irradiance estimation and statistically 
derived parameters needed for sizing of both aircraft and solar cells. The 
technolog y is imp roving rapidly, and current data for various efficiencies 
and other parameters can be found online and from com pany sources.

Previous chapters introduced "S izing" as the process which calculates 
how big and heavy the as-yet-u ndrawn aircraft must be to attain the required 
mission range carrying the design payload. The methods used for fuel­
burning engines begin with an indirect estimation of the fuel burn using a 
ratio between each mission segment's starting and ending weight, called 
the mis sion segment weight fraction (W i/Wi- 1 ). The most important ones 
are based on the Breguet range and loiter equat ions, found by integrating 
the vehicle weight change as fuel is burned (Chapter 17). These ratios are 
then used in an iterative process to find an aircraft takeoff gross weight at 
which there is sufficient fuel weight available to perform the mission.

For battery- electric aircraft a similar method can be defined but the 
Breguet equations are inapplicable. There is no fuel burned, no change in 
weight, and hence no analys is by integration of the change in w eight. 
Inst ead, the required battery mass for each mission segment is developed 
using the equations above, exp ressed as the ratio (mb /m). This ca n be 
called Battery Mass Fraction, or EMF. 
Battery Mass Fraction is the ratio of battery mass to all-up aircraft mass 
(or weight) . The EMF values calculated for the various mission segm ents are 
used in an iterative process descr ibed below in which the fraction of total air­
craft mass available for batteries is comp ared to the battery mass fraction 
required to do the mission. 
EMF has a "talking" resemblance to the Propellant Mass Fraction used in 
rocket analy sis. Like PMF, a high value of EMF is required to obtain good 
range and performance but can only be assured if the vehicle empt y weight 
is kept low. 
Compared to the fuel-burning aircraft analy sis of Chapters 3 and 6, 
EMF is analogous to a value of one minus the mission segment weight 
fraction (1 - Wi/Wi- 1). Ho wever, methods devel oped for fuel-burning air­
craft should not be applied to electric aircraft because their derivations 
assumed that the aircraft gets lighter as the mission segment progresses. 
Instead, we start with the electric aircraft equations found in the previous 
section.

,,..,.. 21 .2 Jet VTOL 
#J f JI Introd uction 
Vert ical-takeoff -and-landing (VTOL) capab ility was pursued almost as 
soon as the je t was invented. The je t engine's high thrust-to-weight ratio 
seems to lend itself to vertical flight, and both military and commerc ial cus­
tomers would be delighted to be able to take off and land without the need for 
long runways. 
To date, there have only been three* operational je t VTOL designs: 
the British Harrier, the Russian YAK 38, and the US F-35B. The first two 
are subsonic aircraft and have limited range. Were it not for their vertical 
flight capabilit y and modern avionics, their overall flight performance 
would place them with aircraft of the mid 19 50's. 
A VT OL aircraft with supersonic capabilities is an orders-of-magnitude 
more difficult chall enge. Although the VTOL Mirage III-V flew at Mach 2 
back in 19 66, it was not considered practical enough for operational develop­
ment. Sim ilarly, the Russian YAK-141 flew at Ml.7 but was cancel led as 
impractical and too expensive. For almost half a 
century after 19 66, not a single supersonic VTOL 
aircraft entered service. 
This is largely because the engine modifications 
and extra equipmen t for VTOL flight impose a huge 
weight penalty. This adds to the aircraft empty 
weight, and that imposes an even greater penalty as a 
result of the leverage effect on sized TOGW . There is 
also the increased internal volume required for the

f lf I I VTOL Term ino logy 
VTOL refers to a capability for vertical takeoff and landing, as opposed to 
conventional takeoff and landing (CTOL). 
An aircraft that has the flexibility to perform either vertical or short 
takeoffs and landings is said to have vertical or short-takeoff -and-landing 
(VSTOL) capab ility. An aircraft that has insufficient lift for vertical flight at 
takeoff weight but that can land vertically at landing weight is called short 
takeoff -vertical land (STO VL) . 
The "tail -sitter" or vertical-attitude-takeoff -and-landing (V ATOL) air­
craft cannot use its vertical lift capability to shorten a conventional takeoff 
or landing roll. In contrast, a horizontal-attit ude-takeoff -and-land (HATOL) 
concept can usually deflect part of its thrust downward while in forward 
flight enabling it to perform a short takeoff and landing (STOL). 
f J f U Fundam ental Problems of VTOL Design 
A number of unique problems characterize the design and operation of 
jet VTOL aircraft. Two fundamen tal problems stand out because they tend 
to have the greatest impact upon the selection of a VTOL propulsion 
concept and upon the design and sizing of the aircraft: balance and thrust 
matching. 
Modern supersonic je t fighters have a T / W exceeding 1. 0, so it would 
seem fairly easy to point the je t exhaust downward and attain vertical 
fl ight. Unfortunately, this is complica ted by the balance problem.

Fig. 21 .1 The balance problem.

Many subsonic je ts and virtually all supersonic je ts are designed with the 
engine at the rear, the cockpit and avionics at the nose, and the pay load 
and fuel near the center of the aircraft. This traditional layo ut places the 
expendables on the e.g., collo cates the parts of the aircraft requiring 
cooling (crew and avionics), and keeps the avionics away from the hot and 
vibrating engine. 
Figure 21.la illustrates this traditional (and usually optimal) layout. If the 
aircraft's thrust exceeds its weight, vertical flight could be obtained simply by 
deflecting the thrust downward, as shown in Fig. 21. lb. However, a "magic 
finger" must hold up the nose to balance the vertical thrust force at the 
tail. This balance problem is possibly the single most impor tant driver of 
the design of the VTOL je t fighter. 
There are really only two conceptual approaches to sol ving the balance 
problem. Either the thrust can som ehow be moved to the e.g. (Fig. 21.lc ), 
or an additional thrust force can be loca ted near the nose (Fig. 21. ld). 
Both of these approaches will tend to compromise the aircraft away from 
the traditi onal and usually optimal layo ut. 
(While Director of Advanced De sign at Lockheed, this author had the 
crazy idea to hold up the nose with gyroscopic flyw heels, like a child's toy. 
A calculation was made of the needed gyroscopic forces. The required fly­
wheels were way too heavy. Crazy Raymer.) 
For cruise-dominated VTOL aircraft such as transports, a more severe 
problem involves thrust matching. If the thrust required for vertical flight 
is provided by the same engines used for cruise, the engines will be far too 
large for ef ficient cruise. 
As an example, imagine designing a VTOL transport using four of the 
TF-39 engines used in the C-5. These produce about 40,000 lb {17 8 kN} of 
thrust at sea-level static cond itions, or 16 0,000 lb {712 kN} altogether. If 

===== PDF PAGE 799 =====
CH APTE R 21 Vertical Flig ht-Jet and Prop 767 
the aircraft is to have a typical 30% thrust surplu s for vertical flight (T / 
W == 1. 3), then the aircraft can weigh no more than 12 3,077 lb {55,827 kg} 
at takeoff. Note that this is far less than the C-5 at 76 4,000 lb {346, 544 kg} . 
Assume a typical cruise L / D of 18 yields a required T / W during cruise of 
about 1/18 , or 0.056. If the aircraft weight at the beginnin g of cruise is about 
95% of the takeoff weight, then the total thrust required during cruise is only 
6,496 lb (1 23,077 x 0.95 x 0.056) {29 kN} . 
This is only 1, 624 lb {7 kN} of thrust per engine, which is about 18% of the 
available thrust for that engine at a typical cruise altitude of 35 ,000 ft 
(1 0,668 m}. It is doubtful that the engine would even run at that low of a 
thrust setting. 
At 35 ,000 ft and Mach 0.9, the best SFC for this engine would be about 
0.73 at a thrust of 9,000 lb {40 kN} per engine. The SFC at the 50% throttle 
setting is about 1. 2 {34 mg /Ns}. This is 64% worse than the SFC at the 
higher thrust setting. If the engine would run at only 18% of its available 
thrust, its SFC would be even worse than the 1. 2 value. 
Aircraft range is dire ctly proportional to SFC. The mismatch be tween 
thrust for vertical flight and thrust for cruise will produce a fuel consumption 
and range penalty for a cruise-domina ted design that uses only the vectored 
thrust of its cruise engines for vertical flight. For this reason, many concep­
tual VTOL transport designs incorporate separate "lift engines" used during 
vertical flight. 
If three of the TF-39 engines in the previous example could be turned off 
during cruise (without a drag penalty), the remaining engine could be oper­
ated at a 72% thrust setting where it gets an SFC of about 0.8 {23 mg/N s}. 
This is a big improvement over all engines being used for both lift and 
cruise. However, the use of separate lift engines introduces additional 
problems, as discussed later. 
There are numerous other problems associated with VTOL aircraft 
design including transiti�n, control, suckdown, hot gas ingestion, FOD, 
inlet flow matching, and ground erosion. These are discussed next following 
a brief discussion of the various VTOL jet propulsion options that are 
currently available to the designer. 
#J f JI VTOL Jet Propulsion Options 
Broa dly speaking, je t VTOL concepts can be divided into those that 
utilize fairly conventional engines and those that use engines modified so 
that the fan and core air are split, with the fan air ducted and exhausted 
from some place separate from the core air. 
The conventional-engine VTOL concepts that do not use additional lift 
engines for vertical flight must have a net takeoff T / W in excess of 1. 0. 
If the je t exhaust is not diverted to some other loca tion for vertical flight, 
the aircraft must either be a tail sitter (V ATOL) or have the engine 
exhaust at the aircraft e.g. and capable of vectoring downward for vertical

flight. This can be accomplished by using a vectoring nozzle or nacelle s that 
tilt (Fig. 21.2). 
The YAK-36 and the X-14 research aircraft had vectoring nozzles at the 
e.g., with the engines out in front. This is prob ably not a good arrangem ent 
for most applications because the cockpit winds up in back, for balanc e, and 
thus does not provide accept able visibil ity for the pilot. Also, in forwar d fli ght 
the je t exhaust scrubs alongside the fuselage, causing thermal and acoustic 
problems. 
An alternat ive approach is to place the nozzles at the center of gravity and 
put the engine in the rear fuselage as on a regular aircraft, but installed back­
ward ! This RIVET concept offers design simplic ity, reduced weight, ease of 
transition, and inherent vectoring in forward flight (VIFF). However, inl et 
duct losses of 5% or more will be caused by the 180-deg bend required 
to supply air to a backwards engine. Sizing studies [13 0, 14 2] indicate 
that, despite these duct losses, RIVE T offers a viable option for supersonic 
V/STOL. 
Tilt nacelles, although heavy, might be the best compromise for some 
applicat ions. Grumman pursued a tilt-nacelle concept for naval applicatio ns 
for a number of years, even flying a subscale model. 
Some VTOL concepts provide a means of diverting the exhaust flow to 
gain vertical lift. This is gene rally done by a retracting blocker device in 
the engine that shuts off the flow through the rearward-facing nozzle. The 
flow is then diverted for ward through internal ducting (Fig. 21 .3).

The diverted flow can be exhausted directly downwards, or it can be "aug­
mented" by either a gas-driven fan or an ejector. Bot h of these can increase 
the thrust obtained from the diverted flow by using the energy of the 
exhaust flow to accelera te a larger mass of air. This augments thrust by 
increasing the propulsi ve ef ficie ncy, as explained by Eq, (1 3. 4) , 
The gas-driven fan is a ducted fan that is turned by turbine blades spun 
by diverted engine exhaust or sometimes, diverted com pressor air. The gas­
driven fan's turbine blades can be inside the fan or out at the tips of the fan 
blades, in which case it is sometimes called a tip-driven fan. 
The Ryan XV-SA used tip-driven fans and attained an "augmentation 
ratio" of almost three, that is, the lifting thrust attained with the tip-driven 
fans was almost three times the thrust produced by the je t engines alone. 
This is prob ably the highest augmentation ratio ever obtained for a je t 
VTOL design. The XV-SA was being considered for rescue operations 
where its combina tion of high forward speed and hover capab ility would 
be beneficial, but during tests, the dumm y being winched into the airplane 
was somehow blo wn to the top of the wing and sucked into the tip-driven fan.

770 Air craf t Des ign: A Concept ual Appr oach 
The ej ector makes use of the viscosity of the air. Any exhaust je t will 
"drag" along adj acent air molecules, acceler ating the free air in its vicinity. 
The ej ector consists of a short duct with an exhaust stream blowing down 
it. Additional air is pulled by viscosity into the duct , accele rated, and 
ejected through a nozzle. This produces thrust greater than the thrust due 
to the je t exhaust alone. 
While ejectors promise theoretical augmentation ratios of 3 or mo re, a 
more realistic value ranges from about 1. 3 to perhaps 2.2. The Roc kwell 
XFV-12 A fe atured ejectors along the entire span of the wing and canard. 
It was expected to produce a high value of augmentation rat io. The actual 
value achieved was only about 1. 5, and it never flew. 
Bot h ejectors and gas-driven fans are heavy and tend to chop up the aircraft 
structure. Also, the internal ducting is bulk y and poses a thermal proble m. 
However, ejectors and gas-driven fans tend to reduce the thrust-matchin g 
problem because the engines do not have to be sized to lift the aircraft by jet 
thrust alone. The resulting imp rovement in cruise fuel consum ption can 
offset the weight of the ejector or gas-driven fan (but prob ably not) . 
One of the simplest ways of providing VTOL capability is to add lift engines 
to an essentially conventional aircraft (Fig. 21. 4). This brute-force approach 
was used in the Mirage III -V. Obviously, the separate lift engines add consider­
able weight and volume to the design, but the forward-flight engine can be 
sized for efficient cruise, thus solving the thrust-matching problem. 
Because the lift engines are designed for a single operating condition, 
they can be highly optimized for that cond ition. Existing lift engines have 
uninstall ed engine T/W on the order of 15, compared to about 6-8 for 
a typical forw ard-flight engine. Future lift engines are expected to have 
engine T / W of 25 or more. Inst allation including door s and a vectoring lift 
nozzle will roughly double the weight. 
The lift- engines -only approach seems rather silly. The airplane has a 
large je t engine for forward flight, but it is turned off for takeoff . If the forward­
flight engine is fitted with some means for vectoring its thrust downward for 
takeoff , then the lift engines can be fewer or smaller. For balance reasons, the 
lift engines will be placed forward, proba bly ju st behind the cockpit. This is 
known as "lift plus lift /cruise" (L + L/C) and was used on the operational 
YAK-38 and the supersonic but ultimately unsuccess ful YAK-141 . 
Numerous studies going back many years have identified L + L/C as a 
good and maybe the best approach for supersonic VTOL. It uses the lift of 
the main engine plus the extra lift of the lift engines (one or more), in a 
design that is not compromised away from a "normal" aircraft configura tion. 
Geor ge Sp angenber g, legen dary director of Naval Air Sy stems Command's 
Eval uation Divis ion, wrote, "If a supersonic V /S TOL fighter capabilit y is 
required, it is probable that the lift plus lift cruise configurat ion is still the 
most promising. " 
A problem with L + L/C: If a lift engine should fail during vertical 
flight or transition, the aircraft would instantly pitch nose down. The

During transition from hover to forward flight, the lift/ cruise engine's

thrust. Because the lift/ cruise engine is at the back of the aircraft, there 
might be a nose-up pitching moment. Probably vectoring should be added 
to the lift engine to impro ve transition. 
If rearward vectoring is added to the lift engine, its thrust can be used to 
return to base in the event that the cruise engine fails. No other VTOL 
approach allows this. 
Perhaps the main problem with L + L/C is that the aircraft operators 
would rather not have to provide maintenance and support for two types of 
engines in one aircraft. This was consid ered a serious disadvantage in the 
early down select for the JSF /F-35 program. However, any choice should be 
based on the maintenance of the total system, and all VTOL concepts have 
problems in this area.

The "shaft-driven lift fan" (SDLF) is bas ically L + L/C , but the fro nt lift 
engine is replaced with a "fan, " which is really more like a je t engine com pres­
sor than a shrouded propeller. This is mechanica lly spun by a driveshaft that 
is powered by an extra turbine in the engine exhaust. For horizo ntal fli ght the 
fan drive is declutched, and the now-unloaded turbine spins free ly. 
Figure 21. 5 shows an early Lockheed SDLF concept [i3o] with stealth 
shaping, and of course, today's F-35B uses SDLF. 
SDLF has many of the bene fits of L + L/C but avoids the higher temper a­
tures and maintenance of a separate lift engine. However, the shaft, clutch, 
gearbox, extra turbine, and the fan all add to the maintenance, which must 
be included in a system-le vel com parison to the other options for jet 
VTOL. Also, the return-to-base capability of L + L/C is lost. 
When the fan is engaged, mechanical power is extracted from the engine 
exhaust and applied to a larger amount of air, augmenting the thrust as 
explained by Eq. (1 3. 4) . Available F-35B data indicate a 1. 4 augmentatio n 
factor, but this augmentation produces less total lift than would be obtained 
by a same-size lift engine.

Interestingly, SDLF is slightly related to a 1956 design called the "Gyro­
ptere," which had four lift fans mechanically powered by a shaft coming 
from a turbine engine. These rotated rearward for forward flight, but the 
design, never bui lt, was found to be clumsy and heavy. Its concept of four­
post vectored thrust actually inspired the invention of the Pegasus engine 
used in the Harrier, described next. 
A number of VTOL propulsion concept s are based upon a "split-f low" 
modific ation to the turbofan engine. The airflow from the fan is split away 
from the core airflow and used in some fashion to address the balance 
and/or thrust-matching pr9blems. 
One such approach exhausts the fan air separately and provides a means 
for vectoring it downward for vertical flight (Fig. 21 .6a). The A V-8 Harrier 
uses the high-bypass Pegasus engine in which the fan air and core air are 
each separately vectored through "elbo w" nozzles (described later) . This 
permits nearly instantaneous vectoring of thrust with no mode changes 
(such as starting a lift engine or diverting air into an ej ector) . This approach 
also simplifies transition and enhances maneu verability. 
On the negative side, the Pegasus-type engine suffers the thrust-matching 
problem because the engine thrust must provide all of the required lifting 
force. Also, the engine must straddle the aircraft e.g. This increases the 
aircraft's cross-sectional area right at the wing loca tion and thus increases 
supersonic wave drag. The successful Harrier is subsonic so this isn't a 
problem. Despi te years of design studies, no viable supersonic configuration 
based on the split-f low approach was ever found. 
It is possible to augment the thrust of such an engine by essentially provid­
ing an "afterburner" for the fan and core airflows in so-called plenum-ch amber 

===== PDF PAGE 806 =====
774 Ai rcraf t Desi gn: A Concep tu al Approach 
burning (PCB). The desirability of such high-temperature exhaust passing next 
to the aircraft skins or blowing down on the landing site is debatable. 
Another means of pr oviding afterburning to the Pegasus-type split fl ow 
engine is to change it to a conventional engine for forward flight, shutting 
off the side nozzles and ducting bo th fan and core air together. Then a con­
ventional afterburner can be added. However, this requires that the engine be 
sized for vertical flight without after burning, leading to penalties in fuel effi ­
cienc y, weight, and cost. 
A close relative of the vectored-thrust split-f low engine is the tandem fan 
(Fig. 21 .6b), a dual-cycle engine that features an additional fan ahead of the 
regular one. During forward flight, the front fan acts to "supercharge" the 
rear fan and engine core. 
For vertical flight the flow from the front fan is diverted by blocker doors 
and exits from a downward -facing front nozzle. Auxili ary doors open to 
provide air to the rear fan and engine core. This has the effect of increasing 
the total amount of air that the engine acts upon and therefore increasing the 
thrust ef ficie ncy. 
The tandem fan is fairly heavy compared to a normal engine, but does 
provide a cle ver means of augmenting the vertical lift and of moving the 
center of vertical lift for ward. The tandem fan engine has a much higher 
effective byp ass ratio when operating in vertical than in forward flight. A 
modified version of the tandem fan called the hybrid fan (Fig. 21.6 c) 
permits the high-byp ass mode to be used in forward flight. 
In the remaining class of jet VTOL propulsion concepts, the engine 
airflow is sp lit, and the fan air is ducted away from the core air (Fig. 21 .7).

engines and eight Rolls Royce lift engines. The noise when hovering must

built, is also unusual in that it never crashed during its flight -test program

#l f JJ Vectoring No zzle Types 
The selection of the type of nozzle -vectoring mechanism is almost as 
important to a VTOL aircraft desi gn as the type of propulsion system. The 
ideal vectorin g mechanism would weigh little more than a conventional 
nozzle and would provide continuous vectoring from 0 to over 90 deg with 
negligible thrust loss. Such a nozzle has yet to be des igned. 
The common types of VTOL nozzle are shown in Fig. 21. 8. The most 
obvious means of vectoring the thrust, vectoring fl aps (Fig. 21 .8a), def lect 
the engine flow much as wi_ng fl aps def lect the external airflow. These vector­
ing flaps can be an integral part of the nozzle system, as shown. This type of 
vectoring system introduces a thrust loss of ro ughly 3-6% when vectored 
90 deg. 
The vectoring fl aps can also be external to the nozzle as a part of the wing 
flap system. This approach was used on the XC-15 transport prototype. 
Although this was not a VTOL aircraft, its wing fl ap system was able to 
turn the engine flow more than 60 deg for STOL landin gs. This, combined 
with a landing gear that permits a 30-deg nose-up position, would provide 
the required 90 deg of total thrust vectoring for vertical flight. 
The bucket vectoring mechanism (Fig. 21.8b) is similar to the commo nly 
used clams hell thrust reverser. The great advantage of this concept is that 
the flow turning fo rces are all carried through the hinge line; thus, the actua­
tor can be fairly small. Also, the bucket can be desi gned with a sm ooth 
turning surface to raise the turning efficienc y. A bu cket vectoring noz zle 
can be desi gned to have a thrust loss of only about 2-3% when vecto red 
90 deg.

Figure 21. 8c shows an axisymmetric vectoring system like that used on 
the Yak-41 and F-35B. The round tailp ipe is broken along slanted lines 
into three pieces, as shown. The three pieces are conn ected with circular 
rotating-ring bea rings so that the middle (shaded) piece can be rotated 
about its lo ngitudinal axis while the other parts remain unrotated. This 
causes the middle and end pieces of the tailp ipe to vector downward as 
shown. Because the tailpipe is esse ntially round, it is lighter than other 
forms of VTOL nozzle. This has a 3-5% thrust loss when vectored 90 deg. 
The ventral nozzle (Fig. 21 .8d) is simply a hole in the bot tom of the 
tailpipe leading to a downwa rd-facing nozzle. To force the exhaust out the 
ventral nozzle, the regular exhaust is blocked off with some type of plate 
or door. The ventral nozzle has a thrust loss on the order of 3-6% when 
vectored 90 deg. 
To reduce hot-gas ingestion and damage to the runway, an afterburner is 
not normally used for vertical lift. A ventral nozzle can therefore be placed 
upstream (forward) of the afterburner. This moves the vertical thrust sub­
stantially for ward compared to a vectoring nozzle at the end of the entire 
engine. That helps the balance problem. 
The "elbow" nozzle is used on the Pegasus engine in the highly successful 
A V-8 Harrier. In the elbow nozzle the flow is turned 90 deg outboard (see top 
view in Fig. 21 .8e) . A circular ring bearing conne cts to the movable part of the 
nozzle, which turns the flow 90 deg back to the freest ream direction. To 
vector the flow downward, the ring bearing is rotated 90 deg, as shown.

The elbow nozzle is simple and lightweight and requires a minimum 
of actuator force for vectoring. However, the flow is always being turned 
through a total of 180 deg, even in forward flight. Because of this, the 
engine is always suffering a thrust loss of approxima tely 6-8%. All of the 
other types of vectoring nozzle only impose a thrust loss during vertical flight. 
Another alternative is to provide elbow nozzles that are only used during 
vertical flight. A blocker door like that used for the ventral nozzle can divert 
the airflo w from a conventional nozzle to the elbow nozzles. Like the ventral 
nozzle, the "part-time" elbow nozzles can be located forward of the afterbur­
ner for balance. The use of a conventional nozzle in forward flight saves fuel 
during cruise. This can more than compensa te for the extra nozzle weight. 
#J f II Suckdown and Fount ain Lift 
The VTOL aircraft in hover is not in stagnant air. The je t exhaust that 
supports the aircraft also accelera tes the air mass around it. This entrainment 
is due to viscosity and is strongest near the exhaust plume, producing a 
downward flowfield about the aircraft (Fig. 21 .9a). 
This downward flowfield pushes down on the aircraft with a "vertical 
drag" force equival ent to a loss of typically 2- 6% of the lift thrust. The mag­
nitude of this vertical drag force depends largely upon the relative loca tions of 
the exhaust nozzles and the wing. If the nozzles are right under the wing, the 
entrained airflow will exert a large downward force. 
Figure 21 .9b shows the effect of the ground on the entrained flow field. 
The je t exhaust strikes the ground and spreads outward. This increases the

m ixing be tween the je t exhaust and the adj acent air, which increases the 
entrainment effect. The entrained download (or "suckdown") therefo re 
increases as the ground is approached. 
A single-jet VTOL concept can experience a 30% reduction in effecti ve 
lift due to suckdown. Furthermore, the suckdo wn increases as the ground 
is approached-a very undes irable handling quality! 
Figure 21. 9c shows a VTOL concept with widely separated multi ple 
nozzles near the ground. The je t exhausts strike the ground and spread 
outward. The exhausts meet in the middle. Because there is nowhere 
else to go, they merge and rise upward, forming a "foun tain" under the 
aircraft. 
This fou ntain pushes upward on the aircraft with a magnitude that will 
often cancel the suckdo wn force. The strength of the fountain lift depends 
upon the exact arrangement of the nozzles and the shape of the fuselage. 
Lower-fuselage shaping that makes it more dif ficult for the fountain to 
flow around the fuselage will increase the fountain effect. For example, 
square lower corners are better than round ones. 
Fountain lift increases as the ground is approached. This desirable hand­
ling quality coun ters the undesirable effect of suckdown. 
The fou ntain lift can be increased even more by the use of lift improve­
ment devices (LIDS) (called cushion augme ntation devices in Britain) . 
These are lo ngitudinal strakes located along the lower fuselage corners 
that capture the foun tain (Fig. 21. 9d). LIDS added to the A V-8B increased 
the net vertical lift over 6%. 
#J f 11 Recir cu lation and Hot-Gas Inge stion 
A VTOL aircraft hovering near the ground tends to "drink its own bath­
water." The hot exhaust gases find their way back into the inlet, causing a 
signific ant reduction in thrust. Also, this recirculated air can include dirt 
and other erosion particles that can damage or destroy the engine. In some 
cases, the dirt kicked up by a hovering VTOL aircraft has com pletely 
obscured the pilot's vision. 
Figure 21.1 0 shows the three con tributors to exhaust recirculation: buoy­
ancy, fou ntain, and relative wind. Bu oyancy refers to the natural tende ncy of 
hot gases to rise. The jet exhaust mixes with the ambient air and slows down 
as it moves farther away from the airplane. Eventually, it has slowed enough 
that the outward momentum becomes negligible, and the buo yancy effect 
takes over. The now-warm air rises up around the aircraft and can eventually 
be drawn back into the inlet. 
The bu oyancy effect takes time. It takes about 30 s in hover for the air 
around the Harrier to heat up by 5°C. This 5°C increase in air temperature 
entering the inlet reduces the engine thrust by about 4%. 
If the nozzle arrangement produces a foun tain, the recirculation will be 
greatly increased. This causes additional hot-gas ingestion (HGI) in addition

The third contributor to recirculation, relative wind, can be due to atmos­
