such aircraft. While this concept was concei ved to simply drop a sm art 
bomb on a predetermined GPS coordinate loca tion, it could also carry sur­
veilla nce, reconnaissance, and communications relay equipment for 
alternative missions. 
'fl Derivative Ai rcraft Design 
The desi gn of a derivative of an existing airplane is proba bly the lea st 
innovative thing we designers are called upon to do, but sometimes it takes 
the most innovative thinking. The problem is simple: whatever we are 
trying to do with the modified airplane is constrained by the real ity of the 
existing airplane. For a blank-sheet-of -paper design, if we need a little 
m ore wing span, we can redraw a few lines or type a few commands into 

===== PDF PAGE 896 =====
864 Air craft Design: A Concep tual Approach 
the CAD program. For a derivative design, we need to know if it is fe asible 
and aff ordable to extend the wing span. 
Will the wing center section take the extra load? If not, it needs to be 
strengt hened, which will increase the cost. Does the extended wing tip 
strike the ground in a bad landing? If so, the landing gear legs might need 
lengthening which is nearly imposs ible for most airplanes. If the aircraft 
total weight increases, can the landing gear handle the loads and are the 
tires big enough? Is the rudder big enough to handle the extra y awing 
moments? It goes on and on, and if some real-world constraint is ignored 
or for gotten, the proj ect fails. 
In fac t, you really cannot complete the concept ual design of an aircraft 
derivative until you've taken an in-depth look at some aspects that would 
normally be consi dered a detail design issue, like the stress calcula tions of 
the wing center section. There is a cost step function: it is fairly cheap to 
extend the wing span until you reach the leng th where the extra load requires 
a wing center-section redesign, and then the cost sudden ly goes up a lot. You 
need to know where that is before you can decide how much to extend the 
wing span. There are no top-level, rule-of -thumb estimat ions. You need to 
do the real calcula tions. 
Luck ily, most airplanes have some growth allowances built in. The 
landing gear of new aircraft are usually designed with a 25% increase in 
gross weight, to allow for future growth. There is sometimes extra volume 
in less accessible parts of the aircraft such as near the wing tips, which can 
be converted to fuel tanks if need be. A design might have extra ground clear­
ance to allow for later retrofitting with a bigger propeller or larger turbofan . 
In some cases, a new design will delibera tely have an entire series of pre­
planned product impro vements (P3I) built in, with a clever configuration that 
allows a later fuselage stretch, or winglet addition, or re-engining, etc. A 
similar process is called "spiral developmen t," a term from the soft ware 
indu stry and impl ying a bit less preplanning but a continuous improvement 
process none thel ess. We pilots shudder at any use of the word "spiral" in con­
nection with an aircraft -t he phrase "death spiral" comes to mind! 
Certain aspects of an aircraft create extreme problems for derivative air­
craft. It is very difficult to increase the allowable total aircraft weight for a 
given landing-gear system, once the built-in growth allowance is used up. 
The shock-struts need greater diameter. The strut itself needs to be stronger, 
and the strut forgings are bot h expensive and long-lead fabrication items. 
The tires cannot have their pressure raised to carry the greater load; that 
will damage the runways. If the tires are made larger, they won't fit inside 
the wheel well s. The brakes inside the tires need greater physical size and 
mass to stop the heavier airplane. 
Ground clearance can restrict propeller size or podded engine diameter. 
For an internal je t engine, it is almost impossible to increase the diameter of 
the internal inlet duct. An entire redesign is necess ary, as was done for the 
F-86H and the British Nimrod. 

===== PDF PAGE 897 =====
CH APTE R 23 Design of Unique Air c raft Concep ts 865 
There is the whole issue of "interoperabili ty" with the current fl eet. You 
probably want to use the same material s and fabrication processes, both for 
production and later mainte nance. You would like for the pilots of the 
current airplane to be able to fly the derivative with minimal training and 
hopefully avoid the need for a new "type rating" for the pilots. This requires 
minimal changes to the cockpit controls and instruments, flying qualities, 
and emergenc y procedures. Again, these are all issues that are normally con­
sidered in detail design but must be resolved before the derivative aircraft 
configurati on can be finalized. 
Typical changes for a derivative aircraft include: 
• Increased takeoff gross weight 
• Increased avionics 
• Increased payload weight 
• Additional payload types 
• External fuel and/ or payl oad 
• Increased fuel 
• Increased thrust from current engine . 
• Re-engine (i.e., new engine type) 
• Wing tip or root extension 
• Winglets 
• New wing 
• Fuselage stretch (watch the tail-down ground angle) 
• Sca b-on pods and pallets 
For those of us in conce ptual design, there is a problem when we work on 
a derivative design study. Our analysis tools, suitable for conce ptual design, 
are forced to almost perfectly match the known capabi lities of the original 
airplane. Otherwise, nobod y will belie ve the numbers for the modified air­
plane. This often requires "tweaking" and "fudge-factoring" the analysis 
inputs until the correct answers are obtained. 
Once we have calibrated the analysis to the unmo dified aircraft and can 
match the range and key performance points, we can define the required 
changes to the geometry and est imate the revised aerodynamics including 
the effects of increased wetted area, revised wing planform, and possibl y 
component interf erences. 
We must also estimate the impact of the design changes on the empt y 
weight. This can be difficult, and our usual statistical equations might not 
give us the right answer. The weight of a modified part is greater than the 
weight of that part if designed all new. Often, a simple pounds-per-square­
foot method is better than a sophisticated statistical equation. The best 
answer, though, is a detail weights buildup of the additional parts. 
If there is a change to propulsion, the new values for thrust and SFC must 
be estimated. Next, we calculate range and performance for the modified air­
craft using the above met hods. Hopeful ly, it all seems reasonable; if not, find 
out why! 

===== PDF PAGE 898 =====
866 Air cr aft Des ign: A Concept ual Ap proach 
The estimation of the cost of a derivative aircraft program is very diffic ult. 
You cannot estimate cost by analy zing the revised design as if it were new and 
then analyzing the cost of the original design using the same met hods, then 
subtracting one from the other. This does not work ! Not even the proven 
methods of Chapter 18 can be applied in this fashio n. 
The best cost estimation is through a detailed work-breakdown-structure 
(WBS) buildup, detailing the actual tasks required to fly and produce the air­
craft. This should be done using actual data for the aircraft being mo difie d, 
but this is difficult to obtain. 
A simple cost- estimation method for derivative aircraft design comes fro m 
the RAND Corpor ation, source of the DAPC A method of Chapter 18. A stat­
istical analysis of various derivative proj ects was performed yielding straight 
lines on log-log graph paper. These can be used to estimate the labor hours 
for the new parts of a derivative aircraft (see (16 9] ). While based only upon 
11 mil itary fighters, bom bers, and transports, it seems reasonable for most 
classes of aircraft until be tter data are available. Take no credit for the old 
parts which are "thrown away." Nobod y reimburses you for those "returns. " 
What We've Learned 
Inno vative aircraft con cepts are a lot of fun and are som etimes worthwhile, 
but designers need to study them with a "show-me" mentality focusing on 
weight, wetted area, and trimmed maximum lift.

Int rodu ction 
T his final chapter offers two design examples that illustrate the con­
cepts and methods presented in this book. These are a single-seat aero­
batic homebuilt airplane, and a lightweight supercruise dogfighter. 
These examples illus trate the steps and thought processes used in 
conceptual design covering the extremes from propeller-po wered, fixed -size 
engine design to "rubber .-engine" supersonic design. The diff erences and 
similarities be tween these extremes of design are shown. 
Design requiremen ts for these aircraft were assumed based upon data for 
similar aircraft. These design requireme nts were then treated as if they were 
mandated by some customer and used as the starting point for the design eff ort. 
The examples are designed and analyzed using the methods presented 
in the book. Every effort has been made by the author to develop credible, 
realistic designs and to analyze and optimize them properly. However, no 
claim is made that these are optimal designs or even good designs or that 
all calculations are correct! 
Furthermore, the examples are incomplete in that only the more impor­
tant analysis areas are presented due to space limitat ions. Were the author to 
grade himself in a col lege design course, these examples would rate at most a 
"B. " The "A" students would conduct far more analysis (structures, roll rate, 
e.g. envelopes, etc.) and would ultimately redraw the as-optimized aircraft to 
ensure that the analysis assumptions were realistic.

The first example is designed and analyzed compl etely by hand with 
pocket calculator to show that this initial design process is fully understa nd­
able. The author even fought to show the original hand-written analysis work 
rather than having it typed. Students can go through it and say, " ... anyb ody 
can do that!" 
The only exception to the by-hand rule is that a simple compute r 
program was used for stepping through the sizing iterations. It could have 
been done by hand using the methods of Chapter 3, but life is too short. 
This simple program is available (free) at the author's website, www.aircraft 
design.com or you can quickly write your own. 
The second design example uses hand calculations only for the pre-layout 
activities including initial sizing and selection of T /Wa nd W / S. For the rest 
of the example, the author's RDS- Student program was used. RDS-St udent 
was written to permit students to analyze and, most impor tant, to optimiz e 
their aircraft design in a one-semester class. A user-friend ly impleme ntation 
of the methods of this book, it is available from AIAA either separately or 
bundled with the book. Further infor mation about RDS-St udent and the 
enhanced RDS- Prof essiona l can be found at www.aircraftdesign.com or 
www.aiaa.org. 
The author recommends that students do their initial sizing and other 
pre-layout activities by hand as shown here, before being permitted to use 
RDS- Student or any other "canned" design program. Then, use the computer 
for the laborious "number- crunching" of siz ing, performance, and trade studies.

permits rapid "garage" fabrication of a one-of -a-kind aircraft. Also, the

1.;nAt' 1t K -''+ \.,;Oncepru ai ue s1gn t:xam p1es YU::> 
Lig htweigh t Su percru ise Figh ter 
This second design example is a lightweight fighter, similar to the original 
concept for the F-16 but with newer technologies and additional capabilities. 
It would operate as a cheap, "low-end" complement to the F-22, much as the 
F-16 did for the F-15. De sign requirements reflect assumed impro vements to 
the F-16 's capabilities, with the addition of sustained supersonic cruise on dry 
power ("supercruise") . Also, relatively short takeoff and landing requirements 
are imposed. To avoid unpleas ant conversations with government personnel, 
no attempt was made to apply stealth shaping or treatments but they would 
undo ubtedly be present in an actual aircraft designed for this mission. 
The selected design incorpor ates one unproven technolog y, the variable 
dihedral vertical tail. This author-patented concept [l ?O] purports to control 
the rearward shift in aerodynamic center as the aircraft accelerates to super­
sonic flight by converting from a V tail subson ically to upright vertical tails 
supersonic ally. This reduces trim drag and enhances maneu verabil ity, as 
was found during studies at Ro ckw�ll. However, the obvious weight 
penalty makes it of marginal utility. It is shown here to illustrate how 
designers handle a new technolog y for which no prior experience can be 
applied. And, it's a fun design exam ple! 
Such a technolog y study is very common in early conc eptual design. The 
impact of such a new technolog y on aerod ynamics, weights, propulsion, etc., 
is estimated as best as possible, and the aircraft is sized and optimized. The 
resulting aircraft is then compared to a baseline design that does not incor­
porate the new technolog y to determine if the new idea should be pursued. 
(Homebuilders: don't build this one either!)

AIRCRAFT DE SIGN 
Design An alysis 
From the dimensions and areas measured from the design layout, this 
initial desig n layout of the DR-3 airc raft was analyzed using the methods 
presented in this book. Ana lysis as described below included aerodynamic s, 
weights, prop ulsion, sizing, performa nce, and cost. Also, a TIW- WIS carpet 
plot was prepared to optimi ze the design. The author's RDS -Student 
computer program was used for the "number-crunching ." This analysis 
could have been done by hand like the first design exam ple. Students should 
be capable of ana lysis using only a pocket calcula tor before they are 
permitted to use RDS or any other "canned" computer program. 
RD S-Student is avai lable from AIAA along with this textbook, and 
includes the com plet e DR-3 sam ple design files as described below. RD S­
St udent and the more-powerful RDS -Professio nal are described at the 
auth or 's website, www. aircraftde sign. com, where additional RDS data files 
are available for download . 
Aerodynamic Lift and Drag 
Aerodyna mic analysis inputs to RDS, including surface areas and 
geometry for wings, tails, fuselage, cano py, and boun dary-layer diverter, are 
shown on the next two pag es. Fusela ge and canopy equiv alent diameters 
were determi ned from maximum cross-section areas . Skin friction drag 
analysis assu med fully tur bulent flow over camouflage paint. Dlq for the 
mi ssile was input based upon the AI M-9 data in Fig. 12 .25, and a cannon 
port Dlq of 0.2 was input as a cons tant value from zero to Mach 2. Leakage 
and protuberance drag of six percent was assumed. 
For wave drag analysis, the maximum total cross se ction area was 
est imated at 20.9 squa re feet { 1. 94 sq.m. ), Jess 3.83 for capture area { 0.36 
sq.m. ), or a net of 17 .07 { 1. 58 sq.m. ) squa re feet. A supersonic wave drag 
empirical factor (E wct) of 2.0 was assumed, typica l of an aircra ft designed 
with some attention to area ruling. 
Maximum lift was esti mated by adju sting the airfoil maximum lift for the 
effects of the as sumed automatic le ading-and trailing-edge maneuver flaps. 
For a 64-series airfoil, Ci-max is about 0.8 2, and from Table 12 .1, delta-Y is 
about 1. 28. Using Table 12 .2 the lift adjust ment for trailing-edge plain flaps 
is about 0.9, and for leading-edge flaps, about 0.3. With hinge line angles of 
10 and 39 deg, Eq. (12 .21) gives a delta Ci-max of about 0.82, giving an 
adju sted airfoil Ci-max of 1. 64. For landing, a CL-max value of 1. 8 was ass umed 
based on data for modern fighters with leading edge flaps. 
The following pages include a sample of the parasite drag calcula tion for 
one altitude and velocity, the total par asit e drag as a function of speed and 
altitude, the parameters determined for calculation of drag-due-to-lift factor 
CK'), a plot of the resulting K versus speed and lift coefficient, and drag 
polars and LID ratios for the DR-3.

Weights 
CHAPTE R 24 Concep tu al De sign Ex ampl es 93 1 
AIRCRAFT DESIGN 
Weights analy sis for the DR-3 was done using the fighter equations in 
Chapter 15 , with adju stments for composite material us age as in Table 15 .4. 
The as-drawn takeoff weight of 16, 480 lb {7 475 kg ) was used as the 
structural design weight, with ulti mate load factor of Nz=7.33x 1. 5, or 11. 
Requir ed dimensions and areas, such as the control su rface area for the wing, 
were measured from the drawing. 
The V-tail was analyzed with the horizontal tail statistical equati on, 
because a V-tail is loaded for trim and maneuvers much like a horizontal tail. 
The analysis was based on the true area and aspect ratio of the surface, i.e., 
90 ft2 { 8.4 sq.m }, and A=6.5 (equivalen t). To account for the variable 
dihedral mecha nism and structural requirements, a 200 lb {9 0.7-kg} weight 
penalty was added as a part of the miscella neous empty weight. 
For the landing gear, it was assum ed that landing weight equals design 
takeoff weight, and gear load factor was _ assum ed to be 4. 
For engine cooling it was assu med that a shroud covers the entire engine, 
so the shroud leng th is 14 ft { 4.3 m}. Engine control length was esti mated 
from the drawing as 18 .3 ft {5 .6 m}. To allow for the extra weight of the 
2-D vectoring nozzle, an additional 400 lb { 181. 4 kg } was added to the 
miscella neou s empty weight. 
In the absence of better data, inst alled avionics weight of 990 lb { 449 kg} 
was guessed using Table 11 .6. However, the RDS program requires 
uninstalled avioni cs weight, which it uses to esti mate inst alled avionics 
weight, so Eq. (15 .21) was used to back out an uninstalled weight of 727 lb 
{3 30 kg ). 
The gun was assum ed to always stay with the aircr aft and so was treated 
as an addition to the miscellaneous empty weight of 400 lb { 181. 4 kg }. 
The following pages pro vide the com plete weights assum ptions and 
inpu ts, followed by the resulting su mmary weights statement. The empty 
weight for the as-drawn takeoff weight of 16 ,480 lb {7 475 kg } was 
determined to be 10 947 .2 lb {4 965 .6 kg }, som ewha t above the prelim inary 
predict ion of 10 788 lb { 4893 kg } used for initial sizing. 
Weights esti mation inputs and results are tabul ated below .

Propulsion 
The DR-3 uses the afterb uming turbofan engine in Appendix E. 1, with an 
assumed reduction in specific fuel consum ption (SF C or C) of 20 per cent to 
adjust for "a dvanced technology ." The uninst alled engine, which already 
includes reasonable allowa nces for the installa tion effects of bleed and 
power ext rac tion, was loaded into RDS data arrays of maximum afterbuming 
thrust and SFC, and maximum dry power thru st and SFC . Then inst allation 
values for inlet recovery, inlet drag, and nozzle drag we re input and used to 
calcula te inst alled thru st and SFC throughout the flight envelope. 
The engine was assum ed to be "r ubber," i.e., it could be sc aled to virtu ally 
any size and thrust to meet the thru st needs of the sized aircraft. This is 
common in early design stud ies when we ca n assume that a new engine will 
be designed and built for our aircraft design. Note that one should normally 
scale a "rubber" engine by no more than about 20-30%, and this example 
required far greater sca ling (downwa rd in size). In a real design study, 
learning that the propo sed engine was far too large would lead to selection of 
a different engine, not to a scaling of that engine by a factor of 50% or more ! 
Following are the input ass umpti ons, ana lysis ca lcula tions, and graphs of 
the inst alled thru st and SFC for the unsca led engine. Note that scaling of the 
engine is done duri ng mi ssion sizing for this design exam ple.

Stability and Control 
An advanced fighter concept such as this would use relaxed static 
stability with an active, fully computerized flight control sy stem as described 
in Chapters 11 and 16. For such a concept, early first-order stability and 
control calcula tions are not so critical because the aircraft's handling 
qualities will be determined largely by the computer programming, prov ided 
that basic requirements including tail sizes and e.g. location are met and the 
aircraft has adequately sized control surfaces. 
Tails were sized using historical volume coefficients (Chapter 6) and 
should prove sufficie nt, pending detailed calcula tions and/or wind tunnel 
testing. The wing location was set to give appr oximately the desired stability 
level, in this case slightly negative at subsonic speeds and not too positive 
(i.e. , relaxed stability) at supersonic speed s. From the e.g. esti mated 
previou sly, we can use the first-order methods of Chapter 16 to esti mate 
neutral point and hence, static margin. This was done using RDS-Student, 
with results at M0.6 as detailed below and as graphed below as a function of 
Mach number. As can be seen, this design is just slightly unstable at 
subsonic speeds-good for minimizing trim drag. Superso nically, the design 
is too stable but this analysis does not take into account the variable dihedral 
tails. When brought to an upright posit ion they will destabiliz e the aircraft 
preventing a trim drag penalty-exactly as intended. 
Following the static margin is a subsonic trim plot showin g a slight 
instability. Note that it takes only a small elevator deflection to trim.

AIRCRAFT DESIGN 
Refined Sizing and Perform ance 
Next the DR-3 was sized to the design miss ion and the required 
performance values were calcula ted, using the methods of this book as 
implemented in the RDS -Student com puter program. A detailed mis sion 
model was developed in RDS matc hing the exact mi ss ion pr ofile given with 
the design requiremen ts. Seve ral assum ptions and est im ations were used. 
Takeoff was assumed to consist of five minutes at milita ry (dry) power. 
Cruise was performed at M0. 85 at 45 ,000 ft { 13 716 m}, determined from the 
range optimization plot to maximize range per unit fuel weight used. Best 
loit er speed at sea level was determi ned to be M0. 29, found using the loiter 
optim iza tion plot, which calculates seconds of lo iter per unit fuel weight 
used. A 50 n-miles (9 2.6 km } range credit was as sumed for the descent from 
high-altitude cr uise down to sea level. 
Mis sion sizing, as detailed below, resulted in a re sized takeoff gro ss 
weight of 17 062 lb { 7739 kg }, vs our original as-drawn weight of 16, 480 lb 
(7 475 kg }. This is close r than one would usually hope for, and probably 
reflects luck more than skill ! 
After the mission sizing results are two trade studies, one of the sizing 
effect of a change in range requir ement and one of the effect of an increase 
or decrease in engine fuel cons umpti on. These were automat ically done with 
the RDS -Professio nal program. Howe ver, the se could ha ve been done with 
RDS-Student by parametri cally changing range or SFC and rerunning the 
sizi ng ca lcula tion , recording the resulting sized tak eoff gro ss weights, and 
plott ing the answers in a format simila r to the se. 
Performance calcula tions were done at a com bat weight of 0.89 times 
takeoff weight, which is the wei ght at the end of crui se (beginning of 
combat) . The RDS program was again used to perform the calculations and 
make the graphs, but the sa me results would be obtained using a pock et 
calcula tor and the methods of this book (and a lot of time !). 
Performance calcula tions follow the sizing re sults , including takeoff, 
landing, Ps, turn rate , and accele rati on. Also included are plots of flight 
envelope, specif ic range, rate of clim b, Ps, and turn rate . 
Note that while most performance requirements were met, the 
requirement for accele rati on from M.9 to Ml. 4 in 30 s was not met by the 
baseline DR-3 design ! Eit her the thru st will have to be incr eased, or the 
requirement will have to be relaxed. This is further discussed in the carpet 
plot optimization at the end of this design example.

AIRCRAFT DESIGN 
T/W- W/S Optimization 
Optimization of thrust-to-weight ratio and wing loading was done using 
the carpet plot methods of Chapter 19. Parametric variations of plus-a nd­
minus 10 and 20% were made about the as- drawn baseline of TIW=0.98 and 
W/S =56 lb/f2 {2 73. l kg/sq.m }. RDS was again used. 
For variations in TIW, it was assumed that engine thrust varies directly 
with TIW. Uninstalled engine weight was assum ed to vary by the 1.1 power 
of the relative change in thrust [see Eq. (10 .3)] . The aerodynamic effect of a 
change in TIW, largely the increase in nacelle wetted area, was as sumed to be 
proportional to engine flow path area and therefore proportional to TIW. 
The aerodynamic and weight impacts of variations in WIS were determined 
assuming that wing area varies inversely with wing loading. Tail area was 
varied by the 3/2 power of the relative change in wing area to keep tail 
volum e constant [see Eqs. (6.28 and 6.29)] . The change in wave drag due to 
the change in wing size was esti mated by changing the maximum cross 
sectional area (Amax) proportional to the change in wing area, wei ghted to the 
wing 's baseline percentage of total cross-se ction area. 
For each combination of parametric variations in TIW and WIS (25 in all), 
the RDS input matrices were revi sed. The aircraft was reanalyzed for 
aerodynam ics and weig hts, and the engine thrust was scaled. Then the sizing, 
cost, and performance analysis were rerun as tabulated below. A carpet plot 
was prepared using the RDS -Professi onal program to save time, but could 
have been done by hand. 
The optimum airplane that meets all requirements is shown on the carpet 
plot at the intersection of the lines labeled "2 -Lan ding " and "7 -Accele ration" 
(30 sec.). It weighs 19 ,30 0 lb { 42 18 kg } and has a T/W of I. I and a WIS of 
59 {2 88). This weight is 17% greater than the as-d rawn DR-3 weight, but 
remember that the baseline could not meet the acceleration requirement. By 
relaxing the requirement for acce leration from Mach 0.9 to 1. 4 from 30 s to 
50 s, the weight of an optimal aircraft fully meeting all other requirements 
drops to 15 ,600 lb (7 070 kg }. Also, this changes the optimal TIW to 0.9 and 
wing loading to 54 {2 64 } and is shown at the intersection of the lines "2-
Landin g" and "8 -Acceleration" (50 s). This is a 19 % reduction in sized 
takeoff gross weight from the aircraft that can meet the accele ration 
requirement . This will produce a cons iderable cost savings for the relaxation 
of that one requirem ent. 
Just for fun, the RDS -Profes sional Multiva riable Optimizer was run to 
determine what additional weight savings could be obtained by optimizing 
for sweep, aspect ratio, taper ratio, and thickness as well as T/W and WIS. 
This produced an optimized weight of 15 ,2 42 lb { 69 14 kg }, 2% less than the 
optimum found with a T/ W- WIS carpet plot. This indica tes that the wing 
planform chosen for the DR-3 using the methods of this book was fairly 
close to optimal already. However, this further 2% weight savings is 
obtained for free, result ing just from slight changes to the wing geometry .

Typical Engine 
Performanc e 
Curves 
T his appendix contains performance curves for three different types of 
aircraft engines: an afterburning turbofan, a high-bypass-ratio turbo­
fan, and a turboprop. Although not identical to any currently in pro­
duction, these engines are represen tative of advanced technolog y suitable for 
use in aircraft design studies. The engines may be scaled using the sca ling 
laws presented in Chapter 10. 
These curves were generated using Vers ion 2.0 of the engine -cycle analy­
sis programs ONX and OFFX that are based on the methods contained in the 
AIAA Education Series textb ook, Aircraft Engine Design, by Jack 
D. Mattingly, William H. Heiser, and Daniel H. Daley. Both the textb ook 
and the programs with their user guide are available from the publisher. 
The author would like to thank Jack Mattingly for preparation of these 
engine performance curves. 
Note: All altitudes are in feet.

QUES TIONS 
Following are the author's suggested home work/examination questions for 
each chapter. The exact questions should be changed a bit to ensure that 
the students don't find the answers online ! 
Another option, favored by the author, is to have the students do a com­
plete des ign proj ect similar to the design examples of Chapter 21. This would 
test the students' understanding of the design and analysis methods pre­
sented throughout the book and give them a better picture of the overall 
design process. A sample RFP is included at the end of this section. 
This author recommends that the students work individually for their first 
exposure to aircraft design, each doing an entire design proj ect rather than 
working as a team. This ensures that they will experience the whole design pro­
cess rather than focus on the part of the process that they alread y under stand. 
The author's RDS win_st udent aircraft des ign soft ware program was 
specifically devel oped to reduce the amount of time spent doing "number­
crunching" design analysis. This allows the studen ts to do trade studies 
and carpet plots in a one-semester class, and to conclude their design 
project reports with the improvements they'd make for the "D ash-Two."

whereas a different tyge of person is prob ably better as a des ign analyst.

at both. Choose and defend either beli ef. There is no right answer; your 
grade depends on demon strating an under standing of design.
